candidates.title: Wuben’s Black Friday Flashlights Bring More Than Brightness to the Gift List
candidates.full_text:
Holding your phone under a cabinet gets awkward pretty quickly when you also need both hands to fix something. Dedicated flashlights offer more freedom, especially when their designs account for where the light needs to go. Wuben approaches that problem from three directions with the X4, X5, and X1 Pro, combining adaptable lighting, multiple tools, and higher output in distinctly shaped bodies that serve different routines.

Black Friday brings its own challenge, namely finding gifts that won’t lose their appeal once the wrapping comes off. Wuben’s seasonal promotion puts these three designs in that conversation, with something for the home tinkerer as well as the person who’d happily stay outdoors after sunset. Their appeal starts with familiar needs, but the details give each one a personality beyond the standard cylindrical flashlight.

The Wuben X4 makes a convincing gift because its usefulness doesn’t require much explanation. Its short, rectangular body houses a main beam rated at up to 1,500 lumens, alongside a separate white side light for closer tasks. That gives the same device a role on the walk back to camp and beside an open book afterward, without having to prop a phone against whatever’s handy.

There’s plenty of flexibility in how you position it, too. A magnetic base attaches to suitable metal surfaces, while the standing design and pocket clip offer other ways to leave your hands free. A rotary wheel adjusts brightness, and colored side lighting adds a playful touch around camp. USB-C charging and a replaceable 3,400mAh battery round out a design whose value comes from finding more reasons to use it.

The Wuben X5 takes a different approach to carrying less gear. It combines white light, ultraviolet (UV) light, and a green laser pointer in one narrow body, each with a distinct job. The white beam handles ordinary illumination, while UV helps examine fluorescent markings. The laser lets you indicate a detail during a presentation, bringing three functions together without asking you to carry three separate devices in your bag.

Its CNC-machined aluminum housing has a flat profile that resists rolling away on a work surface, a small detail that makes sense for an inspection tool. A rotary selector handles mode changes, and a dedicated button gives the laser its own control. The rechargeable battery module also has an alternative: AAA backup power, useful when a weekend away stretches beyond your next convenient chance to plug in.

The Wuben X1 Pro heads farther outdoors, where lighting your immediate surroundings and looking down a dark trail call for different beams. Its separate spot and flood optics let you select either pattern or combine them. The combined peak output is rated at 12,300 lumens, but the more interesting design choice is that flexibility: broad coverage while organizing camp, then a focused beam when your attention moves farther away.

Battery access and charging are part of its performance-focused design, too. An accessible compartment holds two replaceable batteries, while USB-C charging supports up to 30W input. A built-in fan helps manage heat, with vents integrated into the angular housing to move air through the body. There’s also 15W power-bank output, giving the flashlight another job when your phone needs a charge during an evening away from an outlet.

With Black Friday turning attention toward gifts, these designs offer a useful way to think beyond another gadget for the drawer. A light that can stay put while you work, combine inspection tools, or switch between near and distant illumination has a clearer place in someone’s routine. Long after the seasonal promotion, there’s still the shelf to repair, the book to finish, and the campsite to pack up.

candidates.title: Dallas just got a taxi with no steering wheel, and it drives itself in for service
candidates.full_text:
Tesla’s Cybercab started carrying public riders in Dallas on Thursday, and the car doing the work has no steering wheel, no pedals and nobody in the driver’s seat, because there isn’t one. Dallas is the second Texas city on the route, after Austin.

The same car is also going on sale to private owners, though only to the invited, and buying one starts with an invitation, not a configurator. It’s home turf from where I sit in Colleyville, close enough that the edge of Tesla’s operating map is now a local question for the whole metro.

Tesla began inviting select customers to order one for personal use at $29,990, with a $1,000 non-refundable deposit and deliveries targeted for December. The invitation came through Tesla’s own Robotaxi account last week, the posted order example puts the first deliveries in Austin, and Tesla hasn’t said how it picked the invited. One vehicle per customer is the limit unless Tesla agrees otherwise.

None of it moves without the subscription, and Tesla’s wording leaves no gap at all: the Cybercab “will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” The plan costs $299 a month with the first month included, it renews monthly until cancelled, Tesla can reprice it with a month’s notice, and a cancelled month isn’t prorated. A car with no steering wheel and no pedals has no manual fallback, so the subscription isn’t an add-on at all. It’s the ignition.

Covered first is the driving itself, since the subscription carries the unsupervised autonomous operation that runs the car inside the geofences Tesla maintains and redraws. Owners set every trip in the Tesla app or on the 21-inch center touchscreen, the only display in the cabin. There’s no other way to move the car, since every control lives in that screen and that app.

Around that core sits the connectivity, Premium Connectivity included, with live traffic, media streaming and Grok, plus remote support around the clock through the app and the screen. Roadside assistance covers flat tires, lockouts and a dead charge, with towing up to about 50 miles to a Tesla service center or the owner’s home, day or night. Tires are covered end to end, with inspections, rotations, replacements and flat repairs all in the plan, end to end.

Upkeep runs longer than the tech list. It keeps going past the tires.

Glass and wear items ride along too, with windshield replacement, cleaning and a water-repellent coating, wiper blade replacement and cleaning, washer fluid refills and cabin air filter replacements all included. The cameras get cleaned as well, lenses wiped and film buildup removed from the forward-facing camera, and regular vehicle inspections are part of the plan.

Oddest line on the list is the service trip. When scheduled work comes due, the car drives itself to a service center with nobody inside, then drives home again after. Remote diagnostics run ahead of the visit, and a car that takes itself in for service is the strongest case Tesla has for the fee.

Insurance isn’t on Tesla’s tab, and neither are registration, charging, parking or general cleaning. Tesla sells its own insurance for owners who want it, though buying it isn’t required and the premium stays the owner’s either way.

Underneath, the warranty reads conventional: four years or 50,000 miles of basic coverage, and eight years or 100,000 miles on the battery and drive unit with at least 70% of battery capacity guaranteed. Every delivered car also arrives with about 250 miles already on the odometer from Tesla’s road testing. Those miles count toward the warranty’s limits.

EPA-estimated range is 279 miles, with up to 123 miles added in 15 minutes of Supercharging at steady highway speed. It measures 176.2 inches long, 69.0 inches wide and 55.4 inches tall. Eight exterior cameras and a cabin camera do the seeing, the exterior lenses carry their own washers, and it wears no side mirrors at all.

Cargo room runs 20.1 cubic feet behind the two seats. USB power delivery runs to 100 watts for the phones and devices riders bring along.

candidates.title: An Outdoor Gym Without the Industrial Look, 3D-Printed From Waste
candidates.full_text:
There are times when I really would want to try going to a gym but all those exercise equipment can be pretty intimidating. It also seems like the people there know how to use it and what they’re doing and there isn’t room for people like me who may make fools of themselves when trying them out. So when I saw this playground that seemingly has exercise equipment that look inviting, I wish there was something like that in my city.

Gym Elements, a collection of public outdoor fitness objects by Rotterdam studio The New Raw, wants to give outdoor fitness a less technical appearance, using bright yellow sculptural shapes and soft curves to make the equipment feel more approachable. This was a project commissioned by the City of Rotterdam and developed in collaboration with Urban Ideals and Humankind. These are installed objects intended as permanent additions to public space and hopefully something that can be adapted to other public spaces as well.

Visually, the collection has a pleasing chunkiness. Broad yellow surfaces fold into upright supports and stepped platforms, with generous curves wrapping around their corners. Fine lines from the printing process remain visible across the surfaces, while larger ribs give the pieces an almost upholstered appearance. I like that the material hasn’t been disguised as wood or polished into anonymity. The texture gives the objects character without requiring decorative flourishes that have nothing to do with their construction.

The project photography helps explain the approach. One person stretches with both palms against an upright element; elsewhere, a child stands on a broad raised platform. Those images suggest different relationships with the same design vocabulary, from deliberate exercise to playful exploration. To my eye, that flexibility is more interesting than making an outdoor version of a familiar gym machine. A useful public object should leave a little room for people to discover it on their own terms.

Location gives that idea some substance. Gym Elements was developed for Yellow Carpet, an initiative connecting existing and new outdoor fitness facilities through a five-kilometer walking and running route, roughly 3.1 miles. Putting exercise stations along a neighborhood loop makes a different proposition from gathering everything behind a gym entrance. People can do a few stretches or add some exercises in the middle of their walk or while hanging out at the park without necessarily scheduling an exercise routine every day.

What material is used to create these equipment is also worth paying attention to. The plastic is made from recycled polypropylene and reports using 480 kilograms, about 1,058 pounds, of recycled material for the project. Recycled content earns more of my attention when it becomes something useful enough to keep around. Making discarded plastic part of a neighborhood infrastructure seems pretty useful and interesting.

The New Raw’s broader production approach also matters. The studio says its products use single-material construction and avoid adhesives, coatings, and complicated material combinations so they can be repaired and reprocessed. It also reuses misprints and production leftovers. Those choices give the recycling story more credibility than recycled content alone, at least as a design strategy. Actual circularity still requires someone to collect and process an object when its working life ends. A recyclable object needs a practical route back.

Public use brings less glamorous responsibilities, too. The studio’s maintenance guidance acknowledges that layered printed surfaces can collect dust and particles, and that outdoor colors may gradually fade despite UV stabilizers. Regular cleaning remains part of the deal. I appreciate those details because attractive public infrastructure needs a maintenance plan as much as a compelling photograph. Bright yellow might catch your attention on day one; keeping the surfaces inviting several years later is another design consideration altogether.

For me, the strongest idea here is allowing exercise equipment to contribute something visually even when nobody is exercising. A neighborhood shouldn’t have to choose between useful fitness infrastructure and objects it enjoys looking at. Gym Elements makes a persuasive case for asking both of the same piece. The real payoff would be a passerby feeling comfortable enough to stop, put down a bag, and give it a try.
